lessons.title: From dominant follicle to LH surge
lessons.objective: Explain the oestradiol feedback switch that triggers the LH surge, follicle selection, and the real variability of ovulation day and the fertile window.
lessons.closing: Ovulation is not a fixed calendar day: the follicular phase varies most, and the fertile window ends on the day of ovulation.

lessons.title: Luteal phase and the “luteal defect” controversy
lessons.objective: Interpret luteal physiology and apply the current position on luteal phase deficiency: no reliable diagnostic test and no proven empiric treatment.
lessons.closing: With a “short” luteal phase or a “low” progesterone, look for treatable causes; don’t label a defect or prescribe progesterone in a natural cycle without proven benefit.

lessons.title: Confirming ovulation and timing hormone tests
lessons.objective: Choose when to confirm ovulation, with which method and on which cycle day, and avoid tests without a clinical question.
lessons.closing: History first; if a test is needed, time it to the next period and make it answer a specific question.

items.title: The feedback switch that triggers the LH surge
items.core: For most of the cycle oestradiol restrains GnRH secretion; at the end of the follicular phase, rising oestradiol switches to stimulating it, producing a GnRH surge and an LH surge that triggers ovulation. [[ref:kauffman-2022-lh-surge]]
items.body:
GnRH neurons lack the steroid receptors that mediate feedback (ERα, progesterone receptor, androgen receptor), so oestradiol acts indirectly, through “upstream” neurons. Kisspeptin neurons are the main candidate: they directly stimulate GnRH neurons, and people lacking kisspeptin or its receptor are infertile. [[ref:kauffman-2022-lh-surge]]

What remains unclear is how the same oestradiol switches from restraining to stimulating: the mechanisms of the switch are poorly understood and much of the detailed data come from rodents. [[ref:kauffman-2022-lh-surge]]
items.recall: What change in oestradiol action triggers the LH surge, and why is it indirect?

rows.text: Rising oestradiol at the end of the follicular phase
Positive feedback (indirect, via neurons such as kisspeptin neurons)

visual.alt: Diagram: in the follicular phase oestradiol exerts negative feedback on GnRH; at the end of the follicular phase rising oestradiol switches to indirect positive feedback, producing a GnRH and LH surge that triggers ovulation.

items.pearl: The same oestradiol restrains or stimulates depending on the time in the cycle: this is the central idea of the HPO axis.

evidence.label: mechanistic
evidence.note: Narrative review; detailed mechanisms mainly from rodents.

items.title: Dominant follicle selection: what is known and what is not
items.core: Generally a single dominant follicle is selected in the mid-follicular phase and ovulates at mid-cycle; the mechanisms of recruitment and selection are not fully elucidated. [[ref:baerwald-2012-folliculogenesis]]
items.body:
There are three models of antral follicle recruitment: continuous recruitment throughout the cycle, a single “cohort” recruited in the late luteal or early follicular phase, or two or three “waves” per cycle. [[ref:baerwald-2012-folliculogenesis]]

Ultrasound evidence increasingly supports several follicular waves per cycle, and in some women a dominant follicle may be selected in anovulatory waves that precede the ovulatory wave. [[ref:baerwald-2012-folliculogenesis]]
items.recall: When is the dominant follicle usually selected, and which recruitment models exist?
items.application: When you explain cycle physiology, present follicle selection as a described process whose mechanisms are still under study, not as a closed scheme.

evidence.label: limited
evidence.note: Narrative review (2012); only the abstract was verified.

items.title: Myth: “ovulation happens on day 14”
items.core: In more than 600,000 cycles recorded in an app, most women did not ovulate on day 14, and differences in cycle length were driven mainly by the follicular phase. [[ref:bull-2019-cycle-characteristics]]
items.body:
Mean follicular phase was 16.9 days; with 25–30-day cycles, 15.2 days, and with 31–35-day cycles, 19.5 days. Mean luteal phase was 12.4 ± 2.4 days: it varies less than the follicular phase, but it does vary. [[ref:bull-2019-cycle-characteristics]]

ASRM describes a typical luteal phase that is relatively fixed at 12–14 days, ranging from 11–17 days. [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]] Mind the source: in the app study ovulation was estimated by an algorithm (basal body temperature and, optionally, urinary LH), not by ultrasound. [[ref:bull-2019-cycle-characteristics]]
items.recall: If a cycle lasts 34 days, which phase mainly explains the difference from a 28-day cycle?

rows.text: Mainly the follicular phase changes (when ovulation occurs)

visual.alt: Diagram: when the cycle is longer or shorter, what mainly changes is the follicular phase, that is, the day of ovulation; the luteal phase varies less.

items.application: As an approximation, to estimate when a patient ovulates count back from the next expected period, not forward from day 1 (the luteal phase also varies).

evidence.label: association
evidence.note: Observational app data (Bull 2019) and ASRM 2026 committee opinion.

items.title: The fertile window: six days ending at ovulation
items.core: In healthy women trying to conceive, conception occurred only with intercourse during a six-day period ending on the estimated day of ovulation. [[ref:wilcox-1995-intercourse-timing]]
items.body:
The probability of conception was 0.10 with intercourse five days before ovulation and 0.33 with intercourse on the day of ovulation itself. Ovulation was estimated from urinary oestrogen and progesterone metabolites in 625 cycles. “Conception” was defined by a rise in urinary hCG (early pregnancy); two thirds ended in a live birth. [[ref:wilcox-1995-intercourse-timing]]

ASRM advises that, if the patient uses a tracking app, you discuss its limitations in accurately predicting the fertile window. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.recall: How many days does the fertile window last, and on which day does it end?
items.application: Intercourse in the days before ovulation also counts: there is no need to hit the exact day.

evidence.label: association
evidence.note: Classic prospective cohort (1995); abstract only verified.

items.stem: Which best describes the mechanism that triggers the preovulatory LH surge?

options.text: Rising oestradiol switches from negative to positive feedback, indirectly, producing a GnRH and LH surge.
options.why: Correct: this is the described model; GnRH neurons lack steroid receptors and the effect goes through neurons such as kisspeptin neurons.

options.text: Oestradiol acts directly on oestrogen receptors on GnRH neurons.
options.why: GnRH neurons lack ERα; oestradiol action is indirect.

options.text: A fall in oestradiol at the end of the follicular phase releases GnRH from restraint.
options.why: It is rising oestradiol, not a fall, that switches to stimulating GnRH.

options.text: Corpus luteum progesterone initiates the LH surge.
options.why: The corpus luteum forms after ovulation; the surge depends on oestradiol positive feedback.

items.explanation: Same oestradiol, opposite effect depending on timing: negative for most of the cycle, positive at the end of the follicular phase. How the switch happens is still under study.

items.stem: A woman with regular 34-day cycles. Which statement about her ovulation is most accurate?

options.text: She ovulates on day 14 like everyone; her luteal phase lasts about 20 days.
options.why: The luteal phase varies much less than the follicular phase; a 20-day luteal phase would fall outside the described range (11–17 days).

options.text: She most likely ovulates later than day 14, because the difference in length is mainly due to the follicular phase.
options.why: Correct: with 31–35-day cycles the mean follicular phase was 19.5 days.

options.text: A 34-day cycle is anovulatory by definition.
options.why: ASRM considers 21–35-day intervals typical of ovulatory women.

options.text: Ovulation always occurs exactly 14 days before menses.
options.why: The luteal phase also varies (mean 12.4 ± 2.4 days in app data; range 11–17 per ASRM).

items.explanation: Counting back from the expected period estimates ovulation better than counting from day 1, although the luteal phase is not identical in everyone either.

items.stem: According to Wilcox et al. (1995), intercourse on which day gave the highest probability of conception?

options.text: Five days before ovulation.
options.why: That was the low end of the window: probability 0.10.

options.text: The day of ovulation.
options.why: Correct: 0.33, the highest value in the six-day window.

options.text: Two days after ovulation.
options.why: Conception occurred only with intercourse in the six days ending on the day of ovulation.

options.text: Six days before ovulation.
options.why: It falls outside the window: conception occurred only with intercourse in the six days ending on the day of ovulation (from five days before).

items.explanation: According to Wilcox 1995, the fertile window is six days ending at ovulation and the probability of conception (measured by urinary hCG, early pregnancy) rises from 0.10 to 0.33 as that day approaches. ASRM summarises peak fecundability as within the 2 days before ovulation: days −2 to 0 have similar probabilities.

items.title: Normal luteal phase: corpus luteum, progesterone and hCG
items.core: Corpus luteum progesterone is essential to establish and maintain pregnancy until the placenta produces enough of it. [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]]
items.body:
Key features per ASRM: the typical luteal phase lasts 12–14 days (range 11–17); in non-pregnancy cycles progesterone peaks 6–8 days after ovulation; it is secreted in pulses in response to LH pulses and can vary up to 8-fold within 90 minutes. [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]]

If implantation occurs, corpus luteum secretion comes to depend on rising hCG; if hCG fails to rise, the corpus luteum fails and progesterone falls. [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]]
items.recall: When does luteal progesterone peak, and why should a single value be interpreted with caution?

rows.text: Implantation: rising hCG sustains the corpus luteum
No hCG: the corpus luteum fails, progesterone falls

visual.alt: Diagram: after ovulation the corpus luteum forms; progesterone peaks 6–8 days later with pulsatile secretion; if implantation occurs hCG sustains the corpus luteum; otherwise the corpus luteum fails and progesterone falls.

items.pearl: Pulsatile secretion = a single progesterone value is a snapshot, not the film.

items.title: “Luteal phase defect”: a contested diagnosis
items.core: Luteal phase deficiency (LPD) is a clinical diagnosis associated with a luteal phase of ≤10 days, but it has not been proven to be an independent entity causing infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss. [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]]
items.body:
Short luteal phases are common in fertile women: in one study 13% of ovulatory cycles had a luteal phase <10 days; in another 18% had <12 days, and although those women were less likely to conceive the following month, their 12-month fecundity was not lower. [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]]

LPD has been associated with hypothalamic amenorrhoea, eating disorders, excessive exercise, weight loss, stress, obesity, PCOS, endometriosis, ageing, thyroid dysfunction and hyperprolactinaemia, among others; those studies define LPD in different ways. [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]]
items.recall: What does ASRM say about LPD as an independent cause of infertility?
items.application: Faced with a short luteal phase, the useful question is not “does she have a luteal defect?” but “is there an underlying cause (energy, thyroid, prolactin…)?”.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ASRM/SREI 2026 committee opinion; scarce, heterogeneous underlying evidence.

items.title: What I would not order to “diagnose” a luteal defect
items.core: No diagnostic test for LPD has been shown to be reliable in the clinical setting or to distinguish fertile from infertile women. [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]]
items.body:
Progesterone: no minimum concentration defines normal or fertile luteal function; in ovulatory cycles, luteal values <10 ng/mL occur 31.3% of the time. Endometrial biopsy: in a multicentre trial of 847 women with regular cycles, 49% of mid-luteal biopsies were “out of phase”, with no difference between fertile and infertile women; histological dating is not recommended. Molecular receptivity markers remain experimental. [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]]

ESHRE agrees: in women investigated for infertility, endometrial biopsy for histological examination is not recommended in the absence of other indications (strong recommendation, low certainty). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: Why do neither isolated progesterone nor endometrial biopsy diagnose LPD?
items.application: If a patient brings a “low progesterone” or an “out of phase” biopsy as the explanation for her infertility, review what was measured, when, and whether it changes management.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ASRM/SREI 2026; ESHRE 2023 (strong, low certainty) for biopsy.

items.title: What I would do with suspected luteal deficiency
items.core: The first step is to correct any underlying condition, such as hypothalamic or thyroid dysfunction or hyperprolactinaemia; if none is identified, treatment becomes empiric and is generally not recommended. [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]]
items.body:
According to ASRM, no treatment for LPD has improved pregnancy rates in natural, unstimulated cycles, and there is no evidence that progesterone benefits fertility in natural cycles or treats LPD. There are no randomised trials of progesterone in women with LPD. Ovulation induction has not been shown to treat LPD either. [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]]

Key distinction: progesterone after fertility treatments is different from supplementing the natural cycle. Any evaluation for underlying causes should begin after shared decision-making. [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]]
items.recall: What is the first step with suspected LPD, and what does ASRM say about progesterone in natural cycles?

rows.text: Cause identified (hypothalamic, thyroid, hyperprolactinaemia…): treat it
No cause: empiric treatment generally not recommended

visual.alt: Diagram: with suspected abnormal luteal function, decide jointly whether to look for causes; if a cause is identified, treat it; if not, empiric treatment is generally not recommended.

items.application: Before prescribing progesterone “for the luteal phase” in a natural cycle, check for a treatable cause and explain that this use has no proven benefit.

items.title: Patient phrase: “I was told my progesterone is low”
items.core: A single progesterone value can confirm that ovulation occurred, but it cannot assess the quality of the luteal phase. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.body:
Suggested answer: “Progesterone rises and falls in pulses through the day, so a single test can't say whether your luteal phase is ‘good’ or ‘bad’. What it can tell us, if done at the right time, is whether you ovulated.” [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]

Then: “There is currently no reliable test for a ‘luteal defect’, and taking progesterone in a natural cycle has not been shown to improve the chance of pregnancy. What is worth doing is checking for a treatable cause, such as thyroid or prolactin.” [[ref:asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency]]
items.recall: What can and cannot a single luteal progesterone value tell you?
items.application: Useful when the patient arrives with progesterone or “luteal phase supplements” recommended on the basis of a single test.

items.stem: Which statement about luteal phase deficiency (LPD) is consistent with the ASRM committee opinion?

options.text: It is a proven independent cause of infertility.
options.why: ASRM states it has not been proven to be an independent entity causing infertility.

options.text: It is diagnosed with an “out of phase” endometrial biopsy.
options.why: Histological dating does not distinguish fertile from infertile women and is not recommended.

options.text: Short luteal phases also occur in fertile, regularly cycling women, and no test reliably distinguishes fertile from infertile women.
options.why: Correct: this summarises the ASRM/SREI 2026 position.

options.text: A luteal progesterone below a fixed threshold defines LPD.
options.why: No minimum progesterone concentration defines normal or fertile luteal function.

items.explanation: LPD is a contested clinical diagnosis: common in cycles of fertile women and without a reliable diagnostic test.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with regular cycles is trying to conceive. Using LH strips she sees about 9–10 days between the surge and her period. No thyroid symptoms, galactorrhoea, or changes in weight or exercise. She asks for progesterone “to lengthen the luteal phase”. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Prescribe vaginal progesterone in the second half of each natural cycle.
options.why: ASRM: there is no evidence that progesterone is beneficial in natural cycles or for treating LPD.

options.text: Explain the uncertainty, decide together whether to look for underlying causes, and not start empiric treatment if none is found.
options.why: Correct: this is the ASRM approach (correct causes; empiric treatment generally not recommended).

options.text: Perform an endometrial biopsy to confirm the defect.
options.why: Histological dating is not recommended: it does not distinguish fertile from infertile women.

options.text: Start ovulation induction to improve the corpus luteum.
options.why: Ovulation induction has not been shown to treat LPD.

items.explanation: A short luteal phase is common even in fertile women; what changes management is finding a treatable cause, not labelling a “defect”.

items.stem: How does ESHRE (2023) grade the recommendation on endometrial biopsy for histological examination in women investigated for infertility?

options.text: Not recommended without other indications; strong, low certainty.
options.why: Correct: strong recommendation with low certainty.

options.text: Suggested in regular cycles; conditional, very low certainty.
options.why: ESHRE does not suggest it; it advises against it without other indications.

options.text: Good practice point in favour of mid-luteal biopsy.
options.why: It is neither a good practice point nor a recommendation in favour.

options.text: Not recommended; strong, high certainty.
options.why: Direction and strength are right, but the certainty assigned is low, not high.

items.explanation: ESHRE and ASRM agree: endometrial dating is not a valid diagnostic tool in the infertility work-up. Strength and certainty are graded separately.

items.title: Do you need to confirm ovulation? Start with the history
items.core: A thorough menstrual history may be all that is required: oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea are enough to establish anovulation, and additional tests only help when the history is indeterminate. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.body:
In ovulatory women cycles are usually regular, every 21–35 days. The prevalence of ovulatory cycles with a normal menstrual history in non-hirsute women is as high as 99.5%, but falls to 60% in eumenorrhoeic women with hirsutism, in whom luteal progesterone should be considered. If the history is indeterminate: luteal progesterone, urinary LH kits or transvaginal ultrasound; basal body temperature and endometrial biopsy are not routinely recommended. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]

ESHRE: with regular cycles, tests to confirm ovulation are not routinely recommended (good practice point); if warranted, urinary LH, ultrasound or mid-luteal progesterone can be used (conditional, very low certainty). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: When is the menstrual history enough, and when would you add an ovulation test?

rows.text: Clearly regular (no hirsutism): ovulation very likely, no routine tests
Oligo/amenorrhoea: anovulation established → look for the cause
Indeterminate (or hirsutism with regular cycles): luteal progesterone, urinary LH or ultrasound

visual.alt: Diagram: start from the menstrual history. If clearly regular without hirsutism, ovulation is very likely and routine tests are not needed. If oligo- or amenorrhoea, anovulation is established and the cause is sought. If indeterminate, or hirsutism with regular cycles, use luteal progesterone, urinary LH or ultrasound.

items.application: Before ordering tests “to see if she ovulates”, ask: would the result change what I am going to do?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ASRM 2021; ESHRE 2023 (GPP and conditional, very low certainty).

items.title: The “day 21” trap: time progesterone to the next period
items.core: Serum progesterone should generally be measured about one week before the expected onset of menses, not on a fixed cycle day such as day 21. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.body:
For ASRM, a progesterone >3 ng/mL is presumptive and sufficient evidence of recent ovulation; because luteal levels can fluctuate sevenfold within a few hours, a single value confirms ovulation but does not assess luteal phase quality. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]

NICE frames the mid-luteal phase as “day 21 of a 28-day cycle”; with prolonged irregular cycles the test may need to be done later (for example, day 28 of a 35-day cycle) and repeated weekly until the next period starts. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: When would you order progesterone to confirm ovulation in a woman with 35-day cycles?

rows.text: Irregular cycle: repeat weekly until the next period

visual.alt: NICE examples: with a 28-day cycle the mid-luteal phase is around day 21; with a 35-day cycle, for example day 28; with irregular cycles the test is repeated weekly until the next period.

items.application: Write “7 days before the expected period” on the request instead of “day 21”, and check the report units before applying any threshold: 1 ng/mL of progesterone ≈ 3.18 nmol/L, so 3 ng/mL ≈ 9.5 nmol/L.
items.pearl: A poorly timed “low” progesterone may speak about the calendar, not the corpus luteum.

items.title: LH strips and basal temperature: what they add and what they don’t
items.core: Urinary LH kits detect the LH surge that precedes ovulation by 1–2 days and provide indirect evidence of ovulation. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.body:
They correlate well with the serum peak, especially with midday or evening urine; in PCOS, a tonically elevated basal LH can cause false positives, and accuracy varies between products, with false positives and negatives. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]

Basal body temperature: ovulatory cycles are usually biphasic, but some ovulatory women do not show a clearly biphasic pattern; given its poor accuracy it is not routinely recommended. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]] NICE is firmer: do not use basal body temperature charts to confirm ovulation because they do not reliably predict ovulation. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: Why can LH strips mislead in PCOS, and what does NICE say about basal temperature?
items.application: If a patient with PCOS uses LH strips, interpret repeated or persistent “positives” with caution before taking them as ovulation.

items.title: Regular cycles and mid-luteal progesterone: guidelines disagree
items.core: NICE recommends offering a mid-luteal progesterone test to confirm ovulation to people being investigated for infertility, even with regular cycles. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
ESHRE, by contrast, suggests not routinely measuring mid-luteal progesterone with regular cycles (conditional recommendation, very low certainty) and considers ovulation confirmation tests non-routine in that setting (good practice point). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

ASRM sits close to ESHRE: the menstrual history may suffice and additional tests are not required when the history is clearly normal or abnormal. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]] The NICE recommendation dates from 2004 (amended 2013), and NICE also notes that regular monthly cycles mean ovulation is likely. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: Where do NICE and ESHRE disagree on mid-luteal progesterone with regular cycles?
items.application: With regular cycles, both options are defensible; if you order it, time it correctly and explain that it confirms ovulation, not “hormonal quality”.
items.pearl: When guidelines disagree with very low certainty, the practical criterion is whether the result will change management.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG257 (1.18.6–1.18.7); ESHRE 2023 (conditional, very low certainty; GPP); ASRM 2021.

items.title: The “full hormone panel”: what to order, when and for whom
items.core: NICE advises against measuring prolactin in all women concerned about their fertility: only with an ovulatory disorder, galactorrhoea or a pituitary tumour; and thyroid function only with symptoms of thyroid disease. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
With irregular cycles, NICE recommends offering serum FSH and LH. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] ASRM: once oligomenorrhoea or anovulation is confirmed (and pregnancy excluded), look for the cause; TSH identifies thyroid disorders and prolactin is indicated with galactorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, but not routinely. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]

Timing: basal FSH is interpreted on cycle day 2, 3 or 4; basal oestradiol should not be used alone to screen for diminished reserve and serves only to interpret a normal FSH. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]
items.recall: When would you order prolactin and thyroid function in a fertility work-up according to NICE?
items.application: Before signing off a “full” panel, link each hormone to a clinical question and a cycle day; if it has neither, drop it.

items.stem: A woman with 35-day cycles. Her “day 21” progesterone is low and she has been told she does not ovulate. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: It confirms anovulation; ovulation induction should be started.
options.why: With 35-day cycles, day 21 probably falls before the mid-luteal phase: the result does not confirm anovulation.

options.text: It indicates luteal deficiency and justifies progesterone in the second half.
options.why: A single value does not assess the luteal phase, and progesterone in natural cycles has no proven benefit.

options.text: It is probably mistimed; repeat about one week before the expected period (e.g. day 28).
options.why: Correct: ASRM advises measuring ~1 week before menses, and NICE gives day 28 of a 35-day cycle as an example.

options.text: Order an endometrial biopsy to date the endometrium.
options.why: Endometrial dating is not valid to assess ovulation or the luteal phase.

items.explanation: Progesterone is timed relative to the next period, not to day 1. A mistimed result diagnoses nothing.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman, regular 27–29-day cycles, no hirsutism or galactorrhoea, no thyroid symptoms. She asks for “a hormone panel to know if I ovulate”. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Three months of basal body temperature charts to confirm ovulation.
options.why: NICE advises against using basal temperature to confirm ovulation; ASRM does not recommend it routinely.

options.text: Prolactin, TSH, FSH, LH, oestradiol and progesterone on the same day.
options.why: Without an indication, NICE does not recommend prolactin or thyroid function, and a single day does not suit phase-dependent hormones.

options.text: Explain that with regular cycles ovulation is very likely; if confirmation were needed, a simple, correctly timed test (luteal progesterone, urinary LH or ultrasound).
options.why: Correct: consistent with ASRM, ESHRE and NICE, which agree that regular cycles suggest ovulation.

options.text: Luteal-phase endometrial biopsy.
options.why: It is not a valid method for assessing ovulation and is not recommended.

items.explanation: The menstrual history is the first ovulation test. A panel without a clinical question or cycle day adds noise, not information.

items.stem: A patient with PCOS and irregular cycles gets several “positive” LH strips in the same cycle. Which explanation is most important to consider?

options.text: She ovulates several times per cycle.
options.why: This is not the explanation ASRM raises; repeated positives do not prove repeated ovulations.

options.text: A tonically elevated basal LH can cause false positives.
options.why: Correct: ASRM warns of false positives in PCOS due to elevated basal LH.

options.text: LH strips are a direct test of ovulation.
options.why: They provide indirect evidence: they detect the surge that precedes ovulation.

options.text: It indicates luteal deficiency.
options.why: LH strips do not assess the luteal phase, and LPD has no reliable diagnostic test.

items.explanation: In PCOS, an LH “positive” is not the same as ovulation; if confirmation is needed, another correctly timed method is advisable.

items.stem: In women with regular cycles, which statement correctly reflects the ESHRE unexplained infertility guideline (2023)?

options.text: It strongly recommends measuring mid-luteal progesterone in all.
options.why: The opposite: it suggests not measuring it routinely (conditional, very low certainty).

options.text: Ovulation confirmation tests are not routinely recommended (good practice point); if warranted, urinary LH, ultrasound or mid-luteal progesterone (conditional, very low certainty).
options.why: Correct: reflects the guideline wording and grading.

options.text: It recommends basal temperature as the method of choice.
options.why: Basal temperature is not among the methods ESHRE proposes.

options.text: It matches NICE exactly in offering mid-luteal progesterone to all.
options.why: That is precisely the point of disagreement: NICE offers it even with regular cycles; ESHRE suggests not doing so routinely.

items.explanation: Distinguish the statement type (GPP vs recommendation) and its certainty: here everything is very low certainty, which explains why guidelines disagree.

items.title: Case: Inés and the “low day-21 progesterone”

steps.text: Inés (fictional case), 33, has been trying to conceive for 7 months. Regular 34–36-day cycles, no hirsutism or galactorrhoea. At another clinic a day-21 progesterone was ordered and reported as “low”, and she was advised vaginal progesterone in the second half of the cycle “for luteal deficiency”. She asks whether she should start it.
First step: review the timing of the sample. With ~35-day cycles, day 21 probably falls before the mid-luteal phase; progesterone is measured about one week before the expected period.

Second step: explain that a single progesterone value confirms ovulation but does not measure luteal “quality”, that there is no reliable test for luteal deficiency, and that progesterone in natural cycles has not been shown to improve pregnancy.

Third step: if ovulation needs confirming, repeat a correctly timed progesterone or use urinary LH or ultrasound. Without thyroid symptoms or galactorrhoea, NICE does not indicate prolactin or thyroid function up front.
Plan: at 33 with 7 months of trying, continue the couple’s work-up plan according to time trying and risk factors, and do not turn a mistimed figure into a diagnosis or a treatment.

asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.title: Testing and interpreting measures of ovarian reserve: a committee opinion
asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.population: Women with and without known infertility assessed with ovarian reserve markers.
asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.finding: AMH and AFC predict oocyte yield in IVF well but are poor independent predictors of reproductive potential; they should not be used as a fertility test, to deny treatment, or to promote planned oocyte cryopreservation.
asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.limitations: Committee opinion (not a GRADE guideline); US context.

asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.title: Fertility evaluation of infertile women: a committee opinion
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.population: Women evaluated for infertility (including single women, same-sex couples, transgender men and non-binary patients seeking treatment); Fertil Steril 2021;116:1255–65.
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.finding: Evaluation at 12 months if <35 and at 6 months if ≥35; more immediate if >40; without delay with a known condition causing infertility. Evaluate both partners at the same time, with at least one semen analysis at onset. Basic work-up: ovulation, structure and patency of the reproductive tract, and semen analysis. With regular 21–35-day cycles, ovulation confirmation is not required (unless hirsutism). Female age is the single most important predictor of fecundity. Laparoscopy, postcoital test, thrombophilia, immunological tests, karyotype, endometrial biopsy, advanced sperm function testing and prolactin are not routine. Menstrual history may suffice to establish an ovulatory pattern; oligo/amenorrhoea establishes anovulation without further ovulation testing. If history is indeterminate: luteal progesterone (≈1 week before expected menses, not a fixed day such as day 21; >3 ng/mL = presumptive evidence of recent ovulation; a single value confirms ovulation, not luteal quality), urinary LH kits (false positives in PCOS) or transvaginal ultrasound. Basal body temperature and endometrial biopsy are not routinely recommended. Prolactin not routine; indicated with galactorrhoea or oligo/amenorrhoea.
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.limitations: Full text read (ASRM PDF). Committee opinion, not a GRADE guideline; US context; no formal strength or certainty grading.

asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.title: Optimizing natural fertility: a committee opinion
asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine; Practice Committee of the Society for Reproductive Endocrinology and Infertility
asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.population: Couples or individuals attempting conception with no evidence of infertility; Fertil Steril 2022;117:53–63.
asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.finding: Monthly fecundability greatest in the first 3 months; relative fertility at 40 about half that of the late 20s/early 30s; semen parameters decline after 35, but male fertility does not appear appreciably affected before ~50. Fertile window: 6 days ending on the day of ovulation; intercourse every 1–2 days gives the highest rates and 2–3 times per week nearly equivalent; do not limit frequency. Position and postcoital routines have no impact; insufficient evidence that a specific diet improves natural fertility.
asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.limitations: Full text read (ASRM PDF). Committee opinion based on expert consensus; most lifestyle data are observational; US context.

asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency.title: Diagnosis and treatment of luteal phase deficiency: a Committee Opinion
asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine and Practice Committee of the Society for Reproductive Endocrinology and Infertility. Fertil Steril 2026;126(4):633-639
asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency.population: Women with suspected luteal phase deficiency (infertility, pregnancy loss) and fertile, regularly cycling women as comparison.
asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency.finding: Luteal phase deficiency (LPD) is a clinical diagnosis associated with a luteal phase ≤10 days; it has not been proven to be an independent entity causing infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss. No test (luteal length, progesterone, endometrial biopsy, molecular markers) reliably distinguishes fertile from infertile women. First correct underlying conditions (hypothalamic, thyroid, hyperprolactinaemia); empiric treatment is generally not recommended; no treatment has improved pregnancy rates in natural cycles.
asrm-2026-luteal-phase-deficiency.limitations: Committee opinion based on scarce, heterogeneous evidence; replaces the 2021 version (Fertil Steril 2021;115(6):1416-23). Full text verified (PDF on the ASRM site; the web page still shows “(2021)” in its title).

baerwald-2012-folliculogenesis.title: Ovarian antral folliculogenesis during the human menstrual cycle: a review
baerwald-2012-folliculogenesis.authors: Baerwald AR, Adams GP, Pierson RA. Hum Reprod Update 2012;18(1):73-91
baerwald-2012-folliculogenesis.population: Review of more than 200 histological, endocrine and ultrasound studies in women.
baerwald-2012-folliculogenesis.finding: The mechanisms of antral follicle recruitment and selection are not fully elucidated; there are several recruitment theories (continuous, one cohort, two or three waves). Generally a single dominant follicle is selected in the mid-follicular phase and ovulates at mid-cycle; evidence for multiple follicular waves per cycle is increasing.
baerwald-2012-folliculogenesis.limitations: Only the abstract was verified; 2012 narrative review.

bull-2019-cycle-characteristics.title: Real-world menstrual cycle characteristics of more than 600,000 menstrual cycles
bull-2019-cycle-characteristics.authors: Bull JR, Rowland SP, Scherwitzl EB, et al. NPJ Digit Med 2019;2:83
bull-2019-cycle-characteristics.population: 612,613 ovulatory cycles from 124,648 users of a fertility app (Natural Cycles); ovulation estimated by an algorithm using basal body temperature and, optionally, urinary LH.
bull-2019-cycle-characteristics.finding: Mean follicular phase 16.9 days and mean luteal phase 12.4 ± 2.4 days; differences in cycle length were driven mainly by the follicular phase. With 25–30-day cycles the mean follicular phase was 15.2 days; with 31–35-day cycles, 19.5 days. For most, ovulation did not occur on day 14.
bull-2019-cycle-characteristics.limitations: App data with algorithm-estimated ovulation (not confirmed by ultrasound or serum hormones); self-selected users; authors affiliated with the app company. Full text verified.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

kauffman-2022-lh-surge.title: Neuroendocrine mechanisms underlying estrogen positive feedback and the LH surge
kauffman-2022-lh-surge.population: Review of neuroendocrine physiology, mainly from rodent models.
kauffman-2022-lh-surge.finding: For most of the cycle oestradiol exerts negative feedback on GnRH; at the end of the follicular phase rising oestradiol switches to positive feedback, producing a GnRH surge and an LH surge that triggers ovulation. GnRH neurons lack steroid receptors: the effect is indirect, with kisspeptin neurons as key candidates. The mechanisms of the switch remain poorly understood.
kauffman-2022-lh-surge.limitations: Narrative review focused on rodents; extrapolation to humans is partial. Abstract and introduction verified.

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.

wilcox-1995-intercourse-timing.title: Timing of sexual intercourse in relation to ovulation. Effects on the probability of conception, survival of the pregnancy, and sex of the baby
wilcox-1995-intercourse-timing.authors: Wilcox AJ, Weinberg CR, Baird DD. N Engl J Med 1995;333(23):1517-1521
wilcox-1995-intercourse-timing.population: 221 healthy women planning pregnancy; 625 cycles with ovulation day estimated from urinary oestrogen and progesterone metabolites.
wilcox-1995-intercourse-timing.finding: Conception occurred only with intercourse during a six-day period ending on the estimated day of ovulation; the probability of conception ranged from 0.10 with intercourse five days before to 0.33 on the day of ovulation.
wilcox-1995-intercourse-timing.limitations: Only the abstract was verified; healthy women without infertility; conception defined by a rise in urinary hCG; 1995 study.
